answer:
Record it the second way: as the wedding gown ending and a new garment beginning, in one event classified as E81 Transformation (and, because a named person deliberately made the new garment, also as E12 Production). Do not record it as an E11 Modification of one surviving object.

WHY THE CRM DECIDES THIS FOR YOU

The v7.3.2 scope note of E6 Destruction states the three-way rule explicitly: (1) if the matter remaining is not documented, model the event solely as E6 Destruction; (2) 'An event should also be documented as an instance of E81 Transformation if it results in the destruction of one or more objects and the simultaneous production of others using parts or material from the original. In this case, the new items have separate identities. Matter is preserved, but identity is not.'; (3) 'When the initial identity of the changed instance of E18 Physical Thing is preserved, the event should be documented as an instance of E11 Modification.' The same instruction is repeated in the scope notes of E11 Modification ('the new items have separate identities') and E12 Production ('matter is preserved, but identity is not').

The 1950s work is squarely case (2). The bodice was unpicked, the silk and lace panels were recut and restitched into a garment of a different kind, and the worn skirt fabric was discarded. The wedding gown therefore did not survive as a unit of documentation, while its substance and much of its structure did. E81 asks exactly for that combination: destruction and creation in one event, where the new thing 'preserves recognizable substance and structure from the first one(s) but has fundamentally different nature or identity'. Here the preserved substance is literal - the same panels.

E80 Part Removal is the trap worth naming, because unpicking a bodice looks like removing parts. Its own scope note closes that door: if the removal 'results in the total decomposition of the original object into pieces, such that the whole ceases to exist, the activity should instead be modelled as an instance of E81 Transformation, i.e., a simultaneous destruction and production.'

THE OPPOSITE ERROR, AND WHY THIS CASE IS NOT IT

E81 must not be used for mere repurposing. The SIG closed Issue 404 by adding to the E81 scope note that 'a change in the use of an object (especially for buildings) does not count as an instance of' a transformation in and of itself, and the published note now reads: 'substantial material changes should justify the documentation of the result as a new instance of E18 Physical Thing and not just the change of function.' A wedding gown simply relabelled 'christening gown' and put in a different drawer would be no transformation at all. Cutting and restitching it is a substantial material change, so this case falls on the E81 side of the line the SIG drew.

THE IDENTITY CRITERION THE SIG ACTUALLY USES

It is not substance, and it is not a threshold of how much material changed. On the Ship of Theseus (thread t1170), Martin Doerr wrote that CRM assumes identity criteria for E19 Physical Object 'based on the continuity of coherence and functionality of the physical thing, and not on its substance', and that a reassembled ship should be 'a new E19 object, because the continuity of functionality is broken'. In the 48th SIG meeting discussion of Issue 509 he made the same point from the other direction: matter may be wholly lost and identity still persist, because what matters is 'the continuity of the physical coherence of the body parts'. Both tests fail for the wedding gown: it was taken apart, part of it was thrown away, and what emerged is not a wedding gown that has been mended but an infant's christening gown. That is a break in coherence and in function.

Doerr also gives the practical tiebreaker - 'The question is more practical, if the users/owners regard and treat it as the same' - and it points the same way. Neither the family nor the collection treats the christening gown as the wedding gown; the wedding gown is remembered through a photograph, not held.

HOW TO WRITE IT

- the 1920s hand-sewn silk wedding gown: E22 Human-Made Object
- the 1950s christening gown: E22 Human-Made Object
- the 1950s alteration: one event, E81 Transformation AND E12 Production, carrying
  - P124 transformed -> the wedding gown
  - P123 resulted in -> the christening gown
  - P108 has produced -> the christening gown
  - P14 carried out by -> the local seamstress
  - P4 has time-span -> the 1950s

The double classification is what the CRM's own examples do, not an embellishment: P123's examples give 'The transformation of the Venetian Loggia in Heraklion into a city hall (E81, E12) resulted in the City Hall of Heraklion (E24). [AND: has produced (P108) the City Hall of Heraklion (E22)]', and the E81 examples give the mummification of Tut-Ankh-Amun as (E81, E12). It is also structurally necessary here. E81 is a subclass of E63/E64, not of E7 Activity, so its applicable-property list offers P11 had participant but no P14 carried out by. To name the seamstress as the agent, and to record her technique (P32/P33) or the commissioning granddaughter's purpose, you need the E12/E11 side of the event. Conversely, P108 has produced is a subproperty of P31 has modified, so instantiating E12 satisfies E11's required property without a separate P31 statement.

WHAT YOU GAIN BY CHOOSING E81 OVER E11

Two object records that remain connected through the event. P123's scope note: 'New items replace the transformed item or items, which cease to exist as units of documentation' and the 'physical continuity between the old and the new is expressed by the links to the common instance of E81 Transformation'. So the catalogue can legitimately hold a record for a garment the collection does not possess - the 1920s wedding gown, whose existence ended in the 1950s, evidenced by the wedding photograph and the fitting notes - alongside the object it does possess, with the transformation between them. Under E11 Modification you would have a single object with two incompatible descriptions and no way to state that the wedding gown ceased to exist, no way to date the end of its existence, and no place to hang the 1920s production separately from the 1950s one.

The discarded skirt fabric needs no modelling: rule (1) of the E6 scope note covers matter remaining from a destruction that is not documented. If you ever did accession a surviving offcut, it would become a second P123 result of the same transformation.

THE LIMIT WORTH STATING TO THE CATALOGUER

CRMbase has no construct for 'phases' or temporal parts of a physical thing, so you cannot record this as one garment in two states. Issue 509 (Modifying art objects) was opened out of precisely this class of question - what to do when an artwork is reworked into something else - and the SIG closed it in 2023 'on the grounds of not having received empirical evidence / datasets that support drafting additional classes'. The pair-of-objects-plus-transformation pattern is therefore the sanctioned answer and the only one, not a workaround. If your collections system needs 'same garment, two states' for retrieval or display, that has to be handled by your own typing and display logic over the transformation link, not by a CRM class.

rejected_alternatives.option: E11 Modification (of the wedding gown alone)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Rule 3 of the E6 Destruction scope note reserves E11 for when 'the initial identity of the changed instance of E18 Physical Thing is preserved'. Here it was not: the bodice was unpicked, the skirt discarded, and the result is a different kind of garment. E11 would leave one object with two irreconcilable descriptions and no way to say the wedding gown ceased to exist or when.

Its own scope note excludes this case: if the removal produces 'the total decomposition of the original object into pieces, such that the whole ceases to exist', it must be modelled as E81 Transformation instead. Unpicking the bodice and discarding the skirt is exactly that.

rejected_alternatives.option: E6 Destruction (of the wedding gown) plus a separate E12 Production (of the christening gown)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Two unlinked events lose the causal and material continuity the CRM wants recorded. Rule 1 of the E6 scope note confines a bare Destruction to cases where the remaining matter is not documented; here it is documented, as the christening gown. E81 with P124/P123 keeps both identities and the link between them in a single event, and P124 transformed is the sibling of P13 destroyed under P93 took out of existence, so nothing is lost by not instantiating E6.

rejected_alternatives.option: E17 Type Assignment / re-typing the same object
rejected_alternatives.why_not: The E81 scope note distinguishes transformations from 're-classifications (documented using E17 Type Assignment)'. Recording the object as now being of type 'christening gown' would assert a change of documentation, not a change in the world, and would misdescribe an event in which silk was cut and restitched.

Nothing was added to a persisting whole; material was taken away and the remainder rebuilt into a different object. Part Addition presupposes an instance of E18 Physical Thing that survives, 'increased, enlarged, or augmented', which is the reading this case rules out.

rejected_alternatives.option: A 'phase' or state construct linking two states of one garment
rejected_alternatives.why_not: No such class exists in CRMbase. Issue 509 explored temporal parts/phases of physical things and was closed in October 2023 without adding classes, for lack of empirical evidence. Proposing one would be inventing model.

siblings_considered.why_not: E6 Destruction is the other subclass of E64 End of Existence that fits an object ceasing to exist, but rule 1 of its own scope note limits a bare Destruction to events whose remaining matter is not documented. Here the matter is documented - it is the christening gown - and the CRM's rule 2 directs such cases to E81, whose P124 transformed does the work of P13 destroyed while also recording what the matter became.

E80 Part Removal is the sibling under E11 Modification that a cataloguer would reach for when a bodice is unpicked, but its scope note explicitly redirects total decomposition of the original, 'such that the whole ceases to exist', to E81 Transformation. It also cannot express the coming-into-existence of the christening gown, which is why E12 (a Beginning of Existence) is needed alongside E81.

E25 Human-Made Feature is the other subclass of E24 Physical Human-Made Thing, and the recut silk and lace panels might tempt one toward it. But E25 inherits from E26 Physical Feature, whose instances 'cannot be separated from the carrier object' and have 'no natural borders that separate them completely in an objective way from the carrier objects'. Both gowns are free-standing objects with exactly the objective physical boundaries E22 requires, and the panels were in fact separated, which is the opposite of a feature.

notes:
Tool friction. (1) `show` requires the angle brackets around a message-id; without them it answers 'No such message' rather than suggesting the fix. (2) Document chunk ids are not visible in the human-readable `docs` output, and `quote` will not accept a heading such as 'E81 Transformation' - I had to re-run `docs ... --json` to learn that the declaration is `crm732#E81` before any quote could be verified. Worth surfacing the chunk id in the plain output. (3) `--raw` did not expand the truncated `docs` snippets; `--json` was the only way to read a full chunk, which is how the numbered three-part decision rule in the v7.3.2 E6 scope note became visible at all - `concept E6` renders it as running prose, where the rule structure is easy to miss even though it is the decisive passage for this case.

One genuine ambiguity I could not settle from the tools: rule 2 of the E6 scope note says such an event 'should also be documented as an instance of E81 Transformation', and 'also' is not disambiguated - in addition to E6, or instead of it? I read it as instead, because no published example of E81 co-classifies E6 (the examples pair E81 with E12, E69, E20, E22), and because P124 transformed sits beside P13 destroyed as a sibling subproperty of P93 took out of existence, i.e. the CRM supplies a transformation-specific analogue of the destruction property. A reader who takes 'also' literally would add E6 to the event; nothing I found rules that out.

Deliberately not proposed: classes for the wedding photograph and the seamstress's fitting notes, since the question asked is the identity decision. For completeness, E81's incoming-property list does show P70 is documented in (E31 Document), so the fitting notes can be attached directly to the transformation event, and they are what makes the vanished wedding gown documentable as a past object at all.

`concept` renders scope notes from v7.1.3 while `docs` serves v7.3.2; for E6 the two differ in structure (prose vs. numbered rules) though not in substance, and I relied on the v7.3.2 declaration.
